statement: Let $H$ be a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) and $T$ a [bounded operator](c:bounded-operator) on $H$. Then $T$ is a [Fredholm operator](c:fredholm-operator) (closed range, finite-dimensional kernel and cokernel) if and only if its image in the [Calkin algebra](c:calkin-algebra) $B(H)/K(H)$ is invertible, that is, $ST - I$ and $TS - I$ are [compact operators](c:compact-operator) for some bounded $S$.

hypotheses.text: The space $H$ is a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space).
The operator $T\colon H \to H$ is [bounded](c:bounded-operator).

conclusion: $T$ is Fredholm exactly when $ST - I$ and $TS - I$ are compact for some bounded operator $S$ on $H$.

proofs.name: Parametrix and Riesz theory
proofs.slogan: Invert $T$ between the complement of its kernel and its range for one direction, and use the Riesz theory of $I + K$ for the other.
proofs.scope: Both directions: steps 1 and 2 prove that a Fredholm operator is invertible modulo compacts, and steps 3 and 4 prove the converse. In finite dimension every operator is Fredholm and compact, so the statement is trivial there.

roles.why: Completeness gives the bounded inverse theorem, and orthogonal complements give the projections onto $\ker T$ and $(\operatorname{ran} T)^\perp$.
Boundedness makes $\ker T$ closed and puts $T$ in $B(H)$, where the Calkin quotient is formed.

steps.slogan: Restrict $T$ to a bijection from $(\ker T)^\perp$ onto its closed range.
steps.detail: If $T$ is Fredholm, $T_0 = T|_{(\ker T)^\perp}$ is a bounded bijection from the [closed subspace](c:closed-subspace) $(\ker T)^\perp$ onto the closed subspace $\operatorname{ran} T$. Both are Hilbert spaces, so the bounded inverse theorem makes $T_0^{-1}$ bounded.

steps.slogan: Extend the inverse by zero and compute the products $ST$ and $TS$.
steps.detail: Let $S = T_0^{-1}$ on $\operatorname{ran} T$ and $S = 0$ on $(\operatorname{ran} T)^\perp$. Then $ST = I - P_{\ker T}$ and $TS = I - P_{(\operatorname{ran} T)^\perp}$, and these [orthogonal projections](c:orthogonal-projection) have finite rank, so they are [compact](c:compact-operator).

steps.slogan: Bound the kernel of $T$ by the kernel of $I + K$.
steps.detail: Let $ST = I + K$ with $K$ compact. Then $\ker T \subseteq \ker(I + K)$, and $K = -I$ on $\ker(I + K)$, so the closed unit ball of $\ker(I + K)$ is compact. By Riesz's theorem $\ker(I + K)$, and so $\ker T$, is finite dimensional.

steps.slogan: Show that the range of $T$ contains the closed finite-codimensional range of $I + K'$.
steps.detail: Let $TS = I + K'$ with $K'$ compact. The Riesz theory of compact operators (the Fredholm alternative) makes $\operatorname{ran}(I + K')$ closed of finite [codimension](c:codimension). Since $\operatorname{ran} T$ contains it, $\operatorname{ran} T$ is the preimage of a subspace of the finite-dimensional quotient $H/\operatorname{ran}(I + K')$, so it is closed of finite codimension.

steps.slogan: Combine both directions into the Calkin criterion for Fredholm operators.
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 2 give a bounded $S$ that inverts a Fredholm $T$ modulo compact operators. Steps 3 and 4 show that such an $S$ forces a finite-dimensional kernel and a closed range of finite codimension, so $T$ is Fredholm exactly when its class in the [Calkin algebra](c:calkin-algebra) is invertible.

concepts.c:hilbert-space: Orthogonal complements and completeness of the Hilbert space build the parametrix.
concepts.c:bounded-operator: The operators live in $B(H)$, whose quotient is the Calkin algebra.
concepts.c:fredholm-operator: The theorem characterizes Fredholm operators by invertibility modulo compacts.
concepts.c:calkin-algebra: Invertibility in the Calkin algebra is the criterion of the theorem.
concepts.c:compact-operator: The defects $ST - I$ and $TS - I$ are compact operators.
concepts.c:closed-subspace: The bounded inverse theorem needs closed subspaces, which are complete.
concepts.c:orthogonal-projection: The finite-rank projections onto kernel and cokernel are the compact defects.
concepts.c:codimension: Finite codimension of the range is half of the Fredholm property.

source.note: The standard proof, as in G. J. Murphy, C*-Algebras and Operator Theory (1990), theorem 1.4.16.

statement: In a linearly [ordered ring](c:ordered-ring) such as $\mathbb{R}$, every element $x \ge -2$ and every [natural number](c:natural-number) $n$ satisfy the [power](c:power) inequality $(1 + x)^n \ge 1 + nx$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is a linearly [ordered ring](c:ordered-ring).
The element $x \in R$ satisfies $x \ge -2$.

proofs.name: Induction in steps of two
proofs.slogan: Prove the cases $n = 0, 1, 2$ directly, then pass from $n + 1$ to $n + 3$ by multiplication with the square $(1 + x)^2 \ge 0$.
proofs.scope: All $n \ge 0$. The steps of two avoid the sign of $1 + x$, which is negative when $-2 \le x < -1$.

roles.why: The order makes squares nonnegative and lets a nonnegative factor keep an inequality.
The bound gives $2 + x \ge 0$, which makes the extra term $(n + 1)x^2(2 + x)$ nonnegative.

steps.slogan: Check the cases $n = 0$, $n = 1$ and $n = 2$ directly.
steps.detail: For $n = 0$ and $n = 1$ both sides are equal. For $n = 2$, $(1 + x)^2 = 1 + 2x + x^2 \ge 1 + 2x$, because a square is nonnegative in an [ordered ring](c:ordered-ring).

steps.slogan: Multiply the case $n + 1$ by the nonnegative square $(1 + x)^2$.
steps.detail: Assume $(1 + x)^{n+1} \ge 1 + (n + 1)x$. Because $(1 + x)^2 \ge 0$, the multiplication keeps the inequality: $(1 + x)^{n+3} \ge (1 + x)^2 (1 + (n + 1)x)$.

steps.slogan: Expand the product and drop the nonnegative terms.
steps.detail: Expansion gives $(1 + x)^2 (1 + (n + 1)x) = 1 + (n + 3)x + (n + 1)x^2 (2 + x) + x^2$. Since $x^2 \ge 0$ and $2 + x \ge 0$, the product is at least $1 + (n + 3)x$.

steps.slogan: Combine the base cases with the step from $n + 1$ to $n + 3$.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give the case $n + 3$ from the case $n + 1$. Starting from the [natural numbers](c:natural-number) $1$ and $2$ of step 1, this reaches every $n \ge 1$, and $n = 0$ is a base case.

concepts.c:ordered-ring: Squares are nonnegative and nonnegative factors keep inequalities in an ordered ring.
concepts.c:natural-number: The exponent runs over the natural numbers, reached in steps of two.
concepts.c:power: The inequality compares the power $(1 + x)^n$ with a linear term.

source.note: mathlib reduces to one_add_le_pow_of_two_add_nonneg and Commute.pow_add_mul_le_add_pow_of_sq_nonneg, which proves the cases 0, 1, 2 and the step from n + 1 to n + 3 with the square (a + b)^2.

statement: For each dimension $N$ there is a number $c_N$ with this property. If $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ is a [bounded set](c:bounded-set) and $\mathcal{F}$ is a family of [balls](c:ball) of positive radius such that every point of $E$ is the center of a ball of $\mathcal{F}$, then $\mathcal{F}$ has $c_N$ subfamilies of [disjoint](c:disjoint-subsets) balls whose union covers $E$.

hypotheses.text: The set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ is [bounded](c:bounded-set).
Every point of $E$ is the center of a [ball](c:ball) of positive radius in $\mathcal{F}$.

conclusion: Some $c_N$ subfamilies of $\mathcal{F}$, each of pairwise disjoint balls, together cover $E$, and $c_N$ depends only on $N$.

formal.difference: The declaration is the measurable consequence: for an s-finite measure on a space with the Besicovitch covering property, one countable disjoint family of admissible closed balls covers almost all of the set. The topological statement here is Besicovitch.exist_disjoint_covering_families, for families with bounded radii in a space without satellite configurations of $N + 1$ points.

proofs.name: Greedy selection and coloring
proofs.slogan: Choose balls greedily with nearly maximal radius, color each ball differently from the earlier balls it meets, and bound the colors by satellite configurations.
proofs.scope: The case of bounded radii and nonempty $E$. If some ball centered in $E$ has radius above $\operatorname{diam} E$, it covers $E$ alone, and $E = \emptyset$ is trivial.

roles.why: Boundedness reduces the problem to bounded radii, so a nearly maximal radius exists at each stage.
Every point of $E$ has a ball, so the selection can go on until every point of $E$ is covered.

steps.slogan: Pick balls one after another, each with radius at least $1/\tau$ times the largest available radius.
steps.detail: Fix $\tau > 1$ and one [ball](c:ball) $B(x, r_x)$ for each $x \in E$, with bounded radii by the scope. At each stage pick an uncovered center $x_i$ with $\tau r_{x_i} \ge \sup\{r_x : x \text{ uncovered}\}$; mathlib runs this by transfinite recursion.

steps.slogan: Stop when no uncovered center remains, so the chosen balls cover the set.
steps.detail: Each stage uses a new point of $E$, so the recursion stops at a stage with no uncovered center. Hence the chosen balls cover $E$, and each chosen center lies outside all earlier chosen balls.

steps.slogan: Give each chosen ball the least color that no earlier chosen ball meeting it has.
steps.detail: Of two balls of one color, the later one meets no earlier ball of its color, so each color class is a family of [disjoint](c:disjoint-subsets) balls. It remains to bound the number of colors.

steps.slogan: Show that a ball that needs color $M + 1$ forms a satellite configuration of $M + 1$ balls.
steps.detail: Such a ball meets $M$ earlier balls with the colors $1, \dots, M$. The greedy choice keeps each center outside the earlier balls and makes a later radius at most $\tau$ times an earlier one, which is the definition of a satellite configuration with parameter $\tau$.

steps.slogan: Bound the size of satellite configurations in $\mathbb{R}^N$ by a volume count.
steps.detail: Rescale so that the last ball is the unit ball at $0$; Füredi and Loeb move all the centers into the ball of radius $2$ with mutual distances at least $1 - \delta$. For $\tau$ close to $1$ this allows at most $m_N \le 5^N$ points, because disjoint balls of radius $1/2$ around points at mutual distance $1$ fit in the ball of radius $5/2$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that at most $m_N$ colors occur, which gives $c_N = m_N$.
steps.detail: A ball that needs color $m_N + 1$ would give a satellite configuration of $m_N + 1$ balls, which step 5 excludes. So the $m_N$ color classes of step 3 are disjoint subfamilies, and they cover $E$ by step 2.

concepts.c:bounded-set: A bounded set lets the proof assume bounded radii.
concepts.c:ball: The cover and the selected subfamilies consist of balls centered in the set.
concepts.c:disjoint-subsets: Each color class must be a family of pairwise disjoint balls.

source.note: mathlib proves the topological theorem by a greedy TauPackage selection and a coloring, and bounds satellite configurations in vector spaces by Besicovitch.isEmpty_satelliteConfig_multiplicity and multiplicity_le (after Füredi and Loeb); the linked declaration is deduced from it.

statement: Every [holomorphic vector bundle](c:holomorphic-vector-bundle) $E$ of rank $r$ on the complex [projective line](c:projective-line) $\mathbb{CP}^1$ is isomorphic to a [direct sum](c:direct-sum) $\mathcal{O}(a_1) \oplus \dots \oplus \mathcal{O}(a_r)$ of the [line bundles](c:line-bundle-o-n) $\mathcal{O}(a)$, and the integers $a_1 \ge \dots \ge a_r$ are unique.

hypotheses.text: The bundle $E$ is a [holomorphic vector bundle](c:holomorphic-vector-bundle) of finite rank $r$ on $\mathbb{CP}^1$.

proofs.name: Line subbundle of maximal degree
proofs.slogan: Split off a line subbundle $\mathcal{O}(a)$ of maximal degree, split the quotient by induction on the rank, and show that the extension splits.
proofs.scope: Existence by induction on $r$, with $r = 0$ the empty sum; uniqueness in the last step. The proof works with algebraic bundles, which GAGA identifies with holomorphic ones.

roles.why: Finite rank allows induction on $r$, and the holomorphic structure gives, through GAGA, the cohomology groups that the proof computes.

steps.slogan: Pass from the holomorphic bundle to an algebraic bundle with the same cohomology.
steps.detail: By Serre's GAGA theorem, holomorphic bundles, maps and [sheaf cohomology](c:sheaf-cohomology) on $\mathbb{CP}^1$ agree with the algebraic ones. Recall $h^0(\mathcal{O}(k)) = \max(0, k + 1)$ and $H^1(\mathcal{O}(k)) = 0$ for $k \ge -1$.

steps.slogan: Choose the largest integer $a$ with a nonzero section of $E(-a)$.
steps.detail: Serre's theorems make $H^0(E(k))$ nonzero for large $k$ and zero for very negative $k$, so for $r \ge 1$ a largest $a$ with $H^0(E(-a)) \ne 0$ exists. Then $H^0(E(-a-1)) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that a nonzero section of $E(-a)$ vanishes nowhere and gives a subbundle $\mathcal{O}(a)$.
steps.detail: If the section vanished at a point $p$, it would be a section of $E(-a) \otimes \mathcal{O}(-p) \cong E(-a-1)$, against step 2. So it gives an [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) $0 \to \mathcal{O}(a) \to E \to E' \to 0$ with $E'$ a bundle of rank $r - 1$.

steps.slogan: Split the quotient by induction and bound its degrees by $a$.
steps.detail: By induction $E' \cong \bigoplus_i \mathcal{O}(b_i)$. Twisting the sequence by $-a-1$ and using $H^0(E(-a-1)) = 0 = H^1(\mathcal{O}(-1))$ gives $H^0(E'(-a-1)) = 0$, so $b_i \le a$ for every $i$.

steps.slogan: Show that the extension splits because its [Ext](c:ext) group vanishes.
steps.detail: The group $\operatorname{Ext}^1(E', \mathcal{O}(a)) = \bigoplus_i H^1(\mathcal{O}(a - b_i))$ is $0$ because $a - b_i \ge 0$. So the sequence splits and $E \cong \mathcal{O}(a) \oplus \bigoplus_i \mathcal{O}(b_i)$.

steps.slogan: Read off the integers $a_i$ from the dimensions of $H^0(E(k))$.
steps.detail: For a [direct sum](c:direct-sum) of line bundles, $h^0(E(k)) = \sum_i \max(0, a_i + k + 1)$. The jumps of this function of $k$ count the $a_i$ that are at least each integer, so the multiset of the $a_i$ depends only on $E$.

concepts.c:holomorphic-vector-bundle: The theorem classifies holomorphic vector bundles on the projective line.
concepts.c:projective-line: The cohomology of $\mathcal{O}(k)$ on the projective line drives every step.
concepts.c:direct-sum: The bundle splits as a direct sum, and dimensions add over the sum.
concepts.c:line-bundle-o-n: The summands are the line bundles $\mathcal{O}(a)$ of the projective line.
concepts.c:sheaf-cohomology: Vanishing of $H^0$ and $H^1$ groups bounds degrees and splits the extension.
concepts.c:exact-sequence: The maximal subbundle gives the exact sequence that the proof splits.
concepts.c:ext: The vanishing Ext group means that the extension is trivial.

source.note: The standard proof by a maximal line subbundle, as in C. Okonek, M. Schneider and H. Spindler, Vector Bundles on Complex Projective Spaces (1980), chapter I, section 2.

statement: Give each of $n \le 365$ people a birthday chosen [uniformly](c:uniform-distribution) and [independently](c:independence) among 365 days. The [probability](c:probability) that two people share a birthday is $p_n = 1 - \prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(1 - k/365)$. Moreover $p_{22} < 1/2 < p_{23}$, so 23 is the least $n$ with $p_n > 1/2$.

hypotheses.text: Each birthday is [uniformly distributed](c:uniform-distribution) over the 365 days.
The birthdays of different people are [independent](c:independence).

proofs.name: Counting and exponential bounds
proofs.slogan: Count the injective assignments of birthdays, then compare the product with exponentials to place $1/2$ between $n = 22$ and $n = 23$.
proofs.scope: The formula for every $n \le 365$ and the two numerical bounds. Since $p_n$ increases with $n$, the bounds make 23 the least such $n$.

roles.why: Uniform birthdays give each day the same probability $1/365$ for each person.
Independence makes the joint law uniform on all $365^n$ assignments.

steps.slogan: Model the outcomes as $365^n$ equally likely assignments of days to people.
steps.detail: By uniformity and independence each assignment of days to the $n$ people has probability $365^{-n}$. So the probability of an event is the [count](c:counting) of its assignments divided by $365^n$.

steps.slogan: Count the assignments in which all birthdays are distinct.
steps.detail: Distinct birthdays form an [injection](c:injection) from the people to the days, and there are $365 \cdot 364 \cdots (365 - n + 1)$ of them. Hence the probability of no shared birthday is $q_n = \prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(1 - k/365)$, and $p_n = 1 - q_n$.

steps.slogan: Bound $q_{23}$ above by $e^{-253/365}$ with the inequality $1 - x < e^{-x}$.
Bound $q_{22}$ below with the inequality $1 - x \ge e^{-x - x^2}$ for $0 \le x \le 1/2$.
steps.detail: This bound on the [exponential function](c:exponential-function) follows from $\ln(1 - x) = -\sum_{j \ge 1} x^j / j \ge -x - x^2$ for $0 \le x \le 1/2$. With $\sum_{k \le 21} k = 231$ and $\sum_{k \le 21} k^2 = 3311$, it gives $q_{22} \ge e^{-231/365 - 3311/365^2} > e^{-0.66} > 1/2$.

steps.slogan: Combine the bounds into $p_{22} < 1/2 < p_{23}$ and use that $p_n$ increases.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give $p_{23} = 1 - q_{23} > 1/2$ and $p_{22} = 1 - q_{22} < 1/2$. Since $q_{n+1} = q_n (1 - n/365) \le q_n$, the [probability](c:probability) $p_n$ increases with $n$, so $p_n < 1/2$ for every $n \le 22$.

concepts.c:uniform-distribution: Uniform birthdays make all assignments equally likely.
concepts.c:independence: Independence makes the joint distribution uniform on assignments.
concepts.c:probability: The theorem computes the probability of a shared birthday.
concepts.c:counting: Probabilities become counts of assignments over the total $365^n$.
concepts.c:injection: Assignments with distinct birthdays are exactly the injections into the days.
concepts.c:exponential-function: Exponential bounds turn the product into a sum that is easy to estimate.

source.note: The classical computation of the birthday problem (a Freek 100 theorem), with elementary exponential bounds in place of a numerical evaluation.

statement: The set $\mathbb{R}$ of [real numbers](c:real-number) has [cardinality](c:cardinal-number) $\mathfrak{c} = 2^{\aleph_0}$, the cardinality of the [power set](c:power-set) of $\mathbb{N}$. Since $2^{\aleph_0} > \aleph_0$, the set $\mathbb{R}$ is not [countable](c:countable-set).

formal.difference: The declaration states only that $\mathbb{R}$ is not countable; the equality $|\mathbb{R}| = 2^{\aleph_0}$ is the separate declaration Cardinal.mk_real.

proofs.name: Cauchy sequences and the Cantor function
proofs.slogan: Bound $|\mathbb{R}|$ above by sequences of rationals and below by a Cantor-type injection of binary sequences, then apply Cantor's theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with the real numbers built as classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals, as in mathlib.

steps.slogan: Map each real number to a Cauchy sequence of rationals that represents it.
steps.detail: Each real is a class of [Cauchy sequences](c:cauchy-sequence) of [rational numbers](c:rational-number), so a choice of representatives is an [injection](c:injection) of $\mathbb{R}$ into $\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbb{N}}$. Hence $|\mathbb{R}| \le \aleph_0^{\aleph_0} = 2^{\aleph_0}$.

steps.slogan: Embed the binary sequences into $\mathbb{R}$ by $b \mapsto \sum_n b_n 3^{-n}$.
steps.detail: If $b \ne b'$ first differ at $n$, with $b_n = 1$ and $b'_n = 0$, the two sums differ by at least $3^{-n} - \sum_{k > n} 3^{-k} = 3^{-n}/2 > 0$. So the map is injective and $2^{\aleph_0} \le |\mathbb{R}|$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two injections into the equality $|\mathbb{R}| = 2^{\aleph_0}$.
steps.detail: Injections in both directions give a [bijection](c:bijection) by the Cantor–Bernstein–Schroeder theorem. Hence $|\mathbb{R}| = 2^{\aleph_0} = \mathfrak{c}$.

steps.slogan: Show $2^{\aleph_0} > \aleph_0$ with the diagonal set of a map $\mathbb{N} \to \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$.
steps.detail: For any map $f\colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$, the set $D = \{n : n \notin f(n)\}$ differs from each $f(n)$ at $n$. So no map from $\mathbb{N}$ onto the [power set](c:power-set) exists, and $2^{\aleph_0} > \aleph_0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $\mathbb{R}$ has cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$ and is not countable.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give $|\mathbb{R}| = 2^{\aleph_0} > \aleph_0$. A [countable set](c:countable-set) has cardinality at most $\aleph_0$, so $\mathbb{R}$ is not countable.

concepts.c:real-number: The theorem measures the size of the set of real numbers.
concepts.c:cardinal-number: The result compares the cardinals $|\mathbb{R}|$, $2^{\aleph_0}$ and $\aleph_0$.
concepts.c:power-set: The power set of $\mathbb{N}$ has cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$ and beats $\mathbb{N}$.
concepts.c:countable-set: Uncountability is the failure of an injection into $\mathbb{N}$.
concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: Cauchy sequences of rationals give the upper bound on $|\mathbb{R}|$.
concepts.c:rational-number: Sequences of rationals form a set of size $2^{\aleph_0}$.
concepts.c:injection: Injections in both directions compare the cardinalities.
concepts.c:bijection: Two opposite injections give a bijection between $\mathbb{R}$ and $2^{\mathbb{N}}$.

source.note: mathlib derives it from Cardinal.mk_real, which bounds #ℝ above through Real.equivCauchy, mk_quotient_le and aleph0_power_aleph0, and below by cantorFunction_injective with c = 1/3, and from Cantor's theorem 𝔠 > ℵ₀.

statement: Let $p$ be a [prime number](c:prime-number) and let $A$ and $B$ be nonempty subsets of the [cyclic group](c:cyclic-group) $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. Then the [sumset](c:sumset) $A + B = \{a + b : a \in A, b \in B\}$ has $|A + B| \ge \min(p, |A| + |B| - 1)$.

hypotheses.text: The modulus $p$ is a [prime number](c:prime-number).
The sets $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ are nonempty.

proofs.name: Induction with e-transforms
proofs.slogan: Induct along an order on pairs of sets and shrink $A$ by e-transforms that keep the sumset inside $A + B$, until $A$ is a point or contains a whole coset.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. mathlib proves it in every group with $p$ replaced by the least order of a nontrivial subgroup, which is $p$ in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$.

roles.why: Primality makes every nonzero element generate the whole group, so a set fixed by a nonzero shift is everything.
Nonempty sets keep the pairs inside the induction and make the sumset at least as large as each set.

steps.slogan: Order the pairs of nonempty sets by $|A + B|$, then by larger $|A| + |B|$, then by smaller $|A|$.
steps.detail: This order is well founded on pairs of nonempty sets, because $|A| \le |A + B|$ and $|B| \le |A + B|$. Assume the bound for every smaller pair.

steps.slogan: Reduce to the case $|A| \le |B|$ and $|A| \ge 2$.
steps.detail: If $|B| < |A|$, the pair $(B, A)$ has the same [sumset](c:sumset) and the same size sum but a smaller first set, so the bound holds for it. If $|A| = 1$, then $|A + B| = |B| = |A| + |B| - 1$.

steps.slogan: Take distinct $a, b \in A$ and treat the case $A + g = A$ for $g = a - b$.
steps.detail: The shift $g = a - b \ne 0$ has $a \in A \cap (A + g)$. If $A + g = A$, then $A$ is a union of [cosets](c:coset) of the [subgroup](c:subgroup) generated by $g$, which is the whole group because $p$ is prime, so $|A + B| = p$.

steps.slogan: Form the e-transforms $(A \cap (A + g), B \cup (B - g))$ and $(A \cup (A + g), B \cap (B - g))$.
steps.detail: Both sumsets lie in $A + B$; for example $x \in A \cap (A + g)$ and $y - g$ with $y \in B$ give $x + y - g = (x - g) + y$. The four set sizes add up to $2(|A| + |B|)$, and $|A \cap (A + g)| < |A|$ when $A + g \ne A$.

steps.slogan: Close the case $A + g \ne A$ by a disjointness count or by the induction hypothesis.
steps.detail: If $B \cap (B - g) = \emptyset$, then $|A + B| \ge |B \cup (B - g)| = 2|B| \ge |A| + |B|$. Otherwise the first transform has size sum at least $|A| + |B|$ and a smaller first set, or the second has a larger size sum; that transform is smaller in the order, and its bound passes to $A + B$.

steps.slogan: Collect the cases into $|A + B| \ge \min(p, |A| + |B| - 1)$ for all pairs.
steps.detail: Steps 2, 3 and 5 cover every pair: a one-point $A$, a set fixed by the shift and the transformed cases. Well-founded induction along the order of step 1 gives the bound for all nonempty $A$ and $B$.

concepts.c:prime-number: A prime order leaves no proper nontrivial subgroup to trap the sumset.
concepts.c:cyclic-group: The sets live in the cyclic group of order $p$.
concepts.c:sumset: The theorem bounds the size of the sumset from below.
concepts.c:coset: A set fixed by a shift is a union of cosets.
concepts.c:subgroup: The subgroup generated by the shift is the whole group.

source.note: mathlib proves cauchy_davenport_minOrder_add for all groups by DeVos's induction with e-transforms (mulETransformLeft, mulETransformRight and their additive forms) and specializes it by ZMod.minOrder_of_prime.

proofs.name: Combinatorial Nullstellensatz
proofs.slogan: Assume a small sumset, build a polynomial that vanishes on $A \times B$ with a nonzero top coefficient, and contradict the Combinatorial Nullstellensatz.
proofs.scope: Steps 1 to 4 treat $|A| + |B| - 1 \le p$; step 5 treats $|A| + |B| > p$, where $A + B$ is the whole group.

roles.why: Primality makes $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ a field and keeps binomial coefficients with top entry below $p$ nonzero.
Nonempty sets give the exponents $|A| - 1, |B| - 1 \ge 0$ and make $A$ meet every $x - B$ in step 5.

steps.slogan: Treat $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ as a field and state the Combinatorial Nullstellensatz.
steps.detail: Since $p$ is prime, $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ is a [finite field](c:finite-field). Alon's Combinatorial Nullstellensatz says that if $f(x, y)$ has degree $s + t$ and a nonzero coefficient of $x^s y^t$, then $f$ is nonzero somewhere on $S \times T$ when $|S| > s$ and $|T| > t$.

steps.slogan: Assume $|A + B| \le |A| + |B| - 2$ and build a polynomial that vanishes on $A \times B$.
steps.detail: Choose $C \supseteq A + B$ with exactly $|A| + |B| - 2$ elements, which is possible since $|A| + |B| - 2 < p$. The [polynomial](c:polynomial) $f(x, y) = \prod_{c \in C}(x + y - c)$ has degree $|A| + |B| - 2$ and vanishes on $A \times B$.

steps.slogan: Compute the coefficient of $x^{|A| - 1} y^{|B| - 1}$ as a binomial coefficient.
steps.detail: The coefficient is the [binomial coefficient](c:binomial-coefficient) $\binom{|A| + |B| - 2}{|A| - 1}$. Its top entry is less than $p$, so it is not divisible by $p$ and is nonzero in the field.

steps.slogan: Contradict the Combinatorial Nullstellensatz with $S = A$ and $T = B$.
steps.detail: With $s = |A| - 1$ and $t = |B| - 1$, step 1 gives a point of $A \times B$ where $f$ is nonzero, against step 2. Hence $|A + B| \ge |A| + |B| - 1$ when $|A| + |B| - 1 \le p$.

steps.slogan: Cover the case $|A| + |B| > p$ and combine the two cases.
steps.detail: For each $x$, the sets $A$ and $x - B$ have sizes adding to more than $p$, so they meet and $x = a + b$ with $a \in A$, $b \in B$. So $A + B$ is the whole group, and with step 4 this gives $|A + B| \ge \min(p, |A| + |B| - 1)$.

concepts.c:prime-number: A prime modulus makes the integers modulo $p$ a field.
concepts.c:cyclic-group: The sets live in the cyclic group of order $p$.
concepts.c:sumset: The polynomial vanishes on the sumset, which is assumed small.
concepts.c:finite-field: The Combinatorial Nullstellensatz needs polynomials over a field.
concepts.c:polynomial: A product of linear factors encodes the sumset as a zero set.
concepts.c:binomial-coefficient: The top coefficient is a binomial coefficient that is nonzero modulo $p$.

source.note: The polynomial proof of Alon, Nathanson and Ruzsa, as in N. Alon, Combinatorial Nullstellensatz, Combinatorics, Probability and Computing 8 (1999), theorem 3.1.

statement: Let $f\colon V \to W$ be a [linear map](c:linear-map) of finite-dimensional vector spaces with [matrix](c:matrix) $A$ in [bases](c:basis) $b$ of $V$ and $c$ of $W$, and matrix $A'$ in bases $b'$ and $c'$. If the columns of $P$ are the $b$-coordinates of $b'$ and the columns of $Q$ are the $c$-coordinates of $c'$, then $A' = Q^{-1} A P$.

hypotheses.text: The map $f\colon V \to W$ is [linear](c:linear-map).
The families $b, b'$ are finite [bases](c:basis) of $V$, and $c, c'$ are finite bases of $W$.

conclusion: $P$ and $Q$ are invertible and $A' = Q^{-1} A P$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the equivalent identity $A = Q A' P^{-1}$, with $Q$ and $P^{-1}$ written as basis matrices, so it needs no inverse. It holds for free modules over any commutative semiring.

proofs.name: Matrices of identity maps
proofs.slogan: Read the change-of-basis matrices as matrices of identity maps, factor the map through them, and multiply the matrices.
proofs.scope: The whole formula. Zero-dimensional spaces give empty matrices, for which the formula holds trivially.

roles.why: Linearity makes the map determined by its matrix and makes matrices of compositions multiply.
Bases give coordinates, so every linear map has a matrix, and the identity maps have the matrices $P$ and $Q$.

steps.slogan: Identify $P$ and $Q$ with matrices of identity maps.
steps.detail: Column $j$ of $P$ holds the $b$-coordinates of $b'_j = \operatorname{id}(b'_j)$, so $P$ is the [matrix](c:matrix) of $\operatorname{id}_V$ from basis $b'$ to basis $b$. In the same way $Q$ is the matrix of $\operatorname{id}_W$ from $c'$ to $c$.

steps.slogan: Show that the matrix of a composition is the product of the matrices.
steps.detail: For [linear maps](c:linear-map) $g$ and $h$, apply $g \circ h$ to a basis vector and expand $h$ of it in the middle basis. The coordinates that result are the entries of the matrix product, so $[g \circ h] = [g][h]$ in matching bases.

steps.slogan: Show that $P$ and $Q$ are invertible, with inverses the matrices of the reverse identity maps.
steps.detail: By step 2, the matrix of $\operatorname{id}_V$ from $b'$ to $b$ times the matrix of $\operatorname{id}_V$ from $b$ to $b'$ is the matrix of $\operatorname{id}_V$ in one [basis](c:basis), the identity matrix. The same holds for $Q$.

steps.slogan: Factor $f = \operatorname{id}_W \circ f \circ \operatorname{id}_V$ and multiply the matrices.
steps.detail: Read $\operatorname{id}_V$ from $b'$ to $b$, $f$ from $b$ to $c$ and $\operatorname{id}_W$ from $c$ to $c'$. Step 2 gives $A' = [\operatorname{id}_W]_{c \to c'} \, A \, P$, and step 3 gives $[\operatorname{id}_W]_{c \to c'} = Q^{-1}$.

concepts.c:linear-map: The formula describes one linear map in two pairs of bases.
concepts.c:matrix: Matrices of identity maps are the change-of-basis matrices.
concepts.c:basis: Each basis fixes coordinates, and changing it changes the matrix.

source.note: mathlib rewrites with basis_toMatrix_mul_linearMap_toMatrix and linearMap_toMatrix_mul_basis_toMatrix, which rest on LinearMap.toMatrix_comp and on reading a basis matrix as the matrix of the identity.

statement: In [polar coordinates](c:polar-coordinates), every [integrable function](c:integrable-function) $f\colon \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies $\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} f(x, y)\, d(x, y) = \int_{(0, \infty) \times (-\pi, \pi)} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\, r \, d(r, \theta)$, where both integrals are taken for [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure).

hypotheses.text: The function $f\colon \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ is [integrable](c:integrable-function).

conclusion: The integral of $f$ over the plane equals the integral of $f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\, r$ over $(0, \infty) \times (-\pi, \pi)$.

formal.difference: The declaration needs no integrability hypothesis, because the Bochner integral of a non-integrable function is $0$ on both sides, and it allows values in any real Banach space.

proofs.name: Change of variables with Jacobian r
proofs.slogan: Remove a null ray from the plane, then apply the change of variables formula to the polar map, whose Jacobian determinant is $r$.
proofs.scope: The whole formula. The polar map is a diffeomorphism only off the ray $\{(x, 0) : x \le 0\}$, which has measure zero.

roles.why: Integrability makes both integrals finite, and the change of variables formula transfers it from one side to the other.

steps.slogan: Discard the ray $\{(x, 0) : x \le 0\}$, a [null set](c:null-set) of the plane.
steps.detail: The closed ray lies in a line, which has [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) $0$, so its removal does not change $\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} f$. The rest is the open set $U = \mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{(x, 0) : x \le 0\}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\Phi(r, \theta) = (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)$ maps $(0, \infty) \times (-\pi, \pi)$ bijectively onto $U$.
steps.detail: Each point of $U$ has a unique radius $r > 0$ and a unique angle $\theta \in (-\pi, \pi)$, given by the argument function. So $\Phi$ is an injective smooth map on $(0, \infty) \times (-\pi, \pi)$ with image $U$.

steps.slogan: Compute the [Jacobian determinant](c:jacobian-determinant) of $\Phi$ as $r$.
steps.detail: The derivative of $\Phi$ has columns $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ and $(-r\sin\theta, r\cos\theta)$. Its determinant is $r\cos^2\theta + r\sin^2\theta = r$, which is positive for $r > 0$, so $|\det D\Phi| = r$.

steps.slogan: Apply the change of variables formula to $\Phi$ on $(0, \infty) \times (-\pi, \pi)$.
steps.detail: For an injective differentiable map on a measurable set $S$, $\int_{\Phi(S)} f = \int_S |\det D\Phi| \, f \circ \Phi$, and one side is integrable exactly when the other is. With steps 1 to 3 this is the formula in [polar coordinates](c:polar-coordinates).

concepts.c:polar-coordinates: The formula rewrites a plane integral in the coordinates $(r, \theta)$.
concepts.c:integrable-function: Integrability makes both sides finite and equal.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: Both integrals are taken for Lebesgue measure, which ignores null sets.
concepts.c:null-set: The excluded ray is a null set, so it does not change the integral.
concepts.c:jacobian-determinant: The Jacobian determinant $r$ is the factor in the polar integral.

statement: A [linear map](c:linear-map) $\Phi\colon M_n(\mathbb{C}) \to M_m(\mathbb{C})$ between matrix [C*-algebras](c:c-star-algebra) is [completely positive](c:completely-positive-map) if and only if its Choi matrix $C_\Phi = \sum_{i,j=1}^{n} E_{ij} \otimes \Phi(E_{ij})$ is [positive semidefinite](c:positive-semidefinite-matrix). Then $\Phi(X) = \sum_{k=1}^{nm} V_k X V_k^*$ for some $m \times n$ matrices $V_k$.

hypotheses.text: The map $\Phi\colon M_n(\mathbb{C}) \to M_m(\mathbb{C})$ is [linear](c:linear-map).

conclusion: $\Phi$ is completely positive exactly when $C_\Phi$ is positive semidefinite, and then $\Phi(X) = \sum_k V_k X V_k^*$.

proofs.name: Choi matrix and Kraus operators
proofs.slogan: Apply $\mathrm{id} \otimes \Phi$ to a rank-one positive matrix for necessity, and read Kraus operators off the eigenvectors of $C_\Phi$ for sufficiency.
proofs.scope: Both directions and the Kraus form. Here $E_{ij}$ are the matrix units and $M_n(M_m(\mathbb{C})) = M_n(\mathbb{C}) \otimes M_m(\mathbb{C})$.

roles.why: Linearity lets the values $\Phi(E_{ij})$ determine $\Phi$ and makes $\mathrm{id}_p \otimes \Phi$ well defined.

steps.slogan: Apply $\mathrm{id}_n \otimes \Phi$ to the positive matrix $\sum_{i,j} E_{ij} \otimes E_{ij}$.
steps.detail: With $v = \sum_i e_i \otimes e_i$, the matrix $\sum_{i,j} E_{ij} \otimes E_{ij} = v v^*$ is positive semidefinite. If $\Phi$ is [completely positive](c:completely-positive-map), $\mathrm{id}_n \otimes \Phi$ keeps it positive, and its image is $C_\Phi$.

steps.slogan: Write the positive Choi matrix as a sum of rank-one terms $w_k w_k^*$.
steps.detail: If $C_\Phi$ is [positive semidefinite](c:positive-semidefinite-matrix), the spectral theorem gives an orthonormal eigenbasis with nonnegative eigenvalues. Scaling the eigenvectors by the square roots of the eigenvalues gives $C_\Phi = \sum_{k=1}^{nm} w_k w_k^*$ with $w_k \in \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^m$.

steps.slogan: Reshape each vector $w_k$ into a matrix $V_k$ and recover $\Phi(X) = \sum_k V_k X V_k^*$.
steps.detail: Write $w_k = \sum_i e_i \otimes V_k e_i$ with $V_k$ an $m \times n$ matrix. The $(i, j)$ block of $w_k w_k^*$ is $V_k E_{ij} V_k^*$, so $\Phi(E_{ij}) = \sum_k V_k E_{ij} V_k^*$, and linearity extends this to all $X$.

steps.slogan: Show that every map $X \mapsto \sum_k V_k X V_k^*$ is completely positive.
steps.detail: For each $p$ and each positive $Y \in M_p(M_n(\mathbb{C}))$, $(\mathrm{id}_p \otimes \Phi)(Y) = \sum_k (I_p \otimes V_k) Y (I_p \otimes V_k)^*$. Each term is a congruence of a positive matrix, so the sum is positive.

steps.slogan: Combine the two directions with the Kraus form.
steps.detail: Step 1 shows that complete positivity makes $C_\Phi$ positive semidefinite. Steps 2 to 4 show that a positive semidefinite $C_\Phi$ gives the Kraus form, and that this form is completely positive.

concepts.c:linear-map: A linear map is determined by its values on the matrix units.
concepts.c:c-star-algebra: Matrix algebras are the finite-dimensional C*-algebras where the theorem lives.
concepts.c:completely-positive-map: The theorem tests complete positivity by one matrix.
concepts.c:positive-semidefinite-matrix: Positivity of the Choi matrix is the criterion and gives the Kraus vectors.

source.note: Choi's proof, M.-D. Choi, Completely positive linear maps on complex matrices, Linear Algebra and its Applications 10 (1975), 285-290.

statement: Let $K$ be a [number field](c:number-field) with $r_1$ real embeddings, $r_2$ pairs of complex embeddings, class number $h$ (the order of the [ideal class group](c:ideal-class-group)), [regulator](c:regulator-of-a-number-field) $R$, $w$ roots of unity and [discriminant](c:discriminant) $d$. Then the [Dedekind zeta function](c:dedekind-zeta-function) $\zeta_K(s)$ has a simple pole at $s = 1$ with [residue](c:residue) $\frac{2^{r_1}(2\pi)^{r_2} h R}{w \sqrt{|d|}}$.

hypotheses.text: The field $K$ is a [number field](c:number-field), a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}$.

conclusion: The residue of $\zeta_K$ at its simple pole $s = 1$ is $2^{r_1}(2\pi)^{r_2} h R / (w \sqrt{|d|})$.

proofs.name: Counting ideals in each class
proofs.slogan: Count the ideals of norm at most $t$ in each ideal class as lattice points in a cone, and turn the count $\kappa t$ into the residue $\kappa$.
proofs.scope: An outline of the lattice-point proof in Marcus's book. Steps 3 and 4 rest on Dirichlet's unit theorem and on the volume and lattice-point computations of the cited chapters; $n = r_1 + 2r_2$ is the degree of $K$.

roles.why: A number field has a finite class group, a unit group of rank $r_1 + r_2 - 1$ and ideals that embed as lattices in $\mathbb{R}^{r_1} \times \mathbb{C}^{r_2}$.

steps.slogan: Split $\zeta_K(s)$ into the partial zeta functions of the $h$ ideal classes.
steps.detail: For $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, $\zeta_K(s) = \sum_{\mathfrak{a}} N(\mathfrak{a})^{-s} = \sum_C \zeta_C(s)$, where $\zeta_C$ sums over the integral ideals of the class $C$. The [ideal class group](c:ideal-class-group) is finite with $h$ elements.

steps.slogan: Turn the ideals of a class into generators of principal ideals inside a fixed ideal.
steps.detail: Fix an integral ideal $\mathfrak{b}$ in the class $C^{-1}$. Then $\mathfrak{a} \mapsto \mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b} = (\alpha)$ matches the ideals of $C$ with the nonzero $\alpha \in \mathfrak{b}$ up to units, and $N(\mathfrak{a}) = |N(\alpha)| / N(\mathfrak{b})$.

steps.slogan: Build a cone that meets each orbit of the unit group in exactly $w$ points.
steps.detail: By Dirichlet's unit theorem the units modulo roots of unity form a lattice of rank $r_1 + r_2 - 1$ in logarithmic coordinates. A cone $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{r_1} \times \mathbb{C}^{r_2}$ over a fundamental domain of this lattice meets each unit orbit in $w$ points, and $\{x \in X : |N(x)| \le 1\}$ has volume $2^{r_1}\pi^{r_2} R$.

steps.slogan: Count the lattice points of $\mathfrak{b}$ in the cone to get about $\kappa t$ ideals of norm at most $t$.
steps.detail: The embedded ideal $\mathfrak{b}$ is a [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) of covolume $2^{-r_2}\sqrt{|d|}\, N(\mathfrak{b})$. Counting its points in $\{x \in X : |N(x)| \le t N(\mathfrak{b})\}$ and dividing by $w$ gives $\#\{\mathfrak{a} \in C : N(\mathfrak{a}) \le t\} = \kappa t + O(t^{1 - 1/n})$ with $\kappa = 2^{r_1}(2\pi)^{r_2} R / (w\sqrt{|d|})$.

steps.slogan: Turn the ideal counts into a simple pole of residue $h\kappa$ by partial summation.
steps.detail: A [Dirichlet series](c:dirichlet-series) whose coefficient sums are $\kappa t + O(t^{1 - 1/n})$ differs from $\kappa\zeta(s)$ by a series that converges for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1 - 1/n$, so it has a simple pole at $1$ with residue $\kappa$. Summing over the $h$ classes gives the residue $h\kappa$, which is the formula.

concepts.c:number-field: The formula relates invariants of one number field.
concepts.c:ideal-class-group: The zeta function splits into one partial sum per ideal class.
concepts.c:regulator-of-a-number-field: The regulator is the volume of the unit lattice in the cone count.
concepts.c:discriminant: The discriminant gives the covolume of the embedded ideal lattice.
concepts.c:dedekind-zeta-function: The theorem computes the residue of the Dedekind zeta function.
concepts.c:residue: The residue at $s = 1$ is the quantity that the formula gives.
concepts.c:lattice-discrete-subgroup: Ideals embed as lattices whose points the proof counts.
concepts.c:dirichlet-series: Partial summation turns ideal counts into the pole of a Dirichlet series.

source.ref: D. A. Marcus, Number Fields, 2nd edition, Universitext, Springer, Cham, 2018, chapters 6 and 7
source.note: Chapter 6 counts the ideals of norm at most t in an ideal class; chapter 7 turns the count into the residue of the Dedekind zeta function.

statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be [Banach spaces](c:banach-space) over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $T\colon X \to Y$ be a [linear map](c:linear-map) whose [graph](c:graph-of-a-function) $\{(x, Tx) : x \in X\}$ is a [closed set](c:closed-set) in $X \times Y$. Then $T$ is continuous.

hypotheses.text: The spaces $X$ and $Y$ are [Banach spaces](c:banach-space) over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
The map $T\colon X \to Y$ is [linear](c:linear-map).
The [graph](c:graph-of-a-function) of $T$ is a [closed set](c:closed-set) in $X \times Y$.

conclusion: $T$ is continuous, that is, a [bounded operator](c:bounded-operator).

formal.difference: The declaration holds over any nontrivially normed field, not only over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.

proofs.name: Inverse of the graph projection
proofs.slogan: The graph is a Banach space, its first projection is a continuous linear bijection onto $X$, and the bounded inverse theorem makes $x \mapsto (x, Tx)$ continuous.

roles.why: Completeness of $X$ and $Y$ makes the graph complete and allows the bounded inverse theorem.
Linearity makes the graph a subspace and the first projection a linear bijection.
A closed subspace of a Banach space is complete.

steps.slogan: Show that the graph $\Gamma$ is a closed subspace of $X \times Y$, hence a Banach space.
steps.detail: Linearity of $T$ makes $\Gamma$ a linear subspace of the [Banach space](c:banach-space) $X \times Y$, and it is closed by hypothesis. A [closed subspace](c:closed-subspace) of a complete space is complete.

steps.slogan: Restrict the first projection to a continuous linear bijection $\pi\colon \Gamma \to X$.
steps.detail: The map $\pi(x, Tx) = x$ is linear with $\|x\| \le \|(x, Tx)\|$, so it is continuous. It is bijective with inverse $x \mapsto (x, Tx)$.

steps.slogan: Make the inverse $x \mapsto (x, Tx)$ continuous by the bounded inverse theorem.
steps.detail: A continuous linear bijection between Banach spaces has a continuous inverse, by the open mapping theorem. So $\pi^{-1}\colon X \to \Gamma$ is continuous.

steps.slogan: Write $T$ as the second projection composed with $\pi^{-1}$.
steps.detail: For each $x$, $Tx$ is the second coordinate of $\pi^{-1}(x)$. The second projection $X \times Y \to Y$ is continuous, so $T$ is continuous and hence a [bounded operator](c:bounded-operator).

concepts.c:banach-space: The bounded inverse theorem needs complete spaces on both sides.
concepts.c:linear-map: Linearity makes the graph a subspace and the projection linear.
concepts.c:graph-of-a-function: The graph becomes the Banach space on which the projection acts.
concepts.c:closed-set: Closedness of the graph is what makes it complete.
concepts.c:bounded-operator: For linear maps, continuity is the same as boundedness.
concepts.c:closed-subspace: A closed subspace of a Banach space is again a Banach space.

source.note: mathlib makes the graph complete (completeSpace_coe_iff_isComplete), builds the linear equivalence from E to the graph and applies LinearEquiv.toContinuousLinearEquivOfContinuous, the bounded inverse theorem, to its continuous inverse.

statement: Let $C$ be a small category and $P\colon C^{op} \to \mathbf{Set}$ a [presheaf](c:presheaf). Then $P$ is the [colimit](c:colimit) of the [representable](c:representable-functor) presheaves $y(c) = \operatorname{Hom}(-, c)$ over the [category of elements](c:grothendieck-construction) of $P$: $P \cong \operatorname{colim}_{(c, x)} y(c)$ over pairs with $x \in P(c)$, where the cocone map $y(c) \to P$ corresponds to $x$ by the Yoneda lemma.

hypotheses.text: The category $C$ is small.
The functor $P\colon C^{op} \to \mathbf{Set}$ is a [presheaf](c:presheaf).

conclusion: The maps $\hat{x}\colon y(c) \to P$ form a colimit cocone, so $P \cong \operatorname{colim}_{(c, x)} y(c)$.

proofs.name: Cocone from the Yoneda lemma
proofs.slogan: Turn each element $x \in P(c)$ into a map $y(c) \to P$, and show that these maps form a universal cocone.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma; the colimit is taken in the category of presheaves on $C$.

roles.why: Smallness makes the category of elements small, so the colimit is a small colimit of presheaves.
The presheaf supplies the elements $x \in P(c)$ and the maps $P(g)$ that index the diagram.

steps.slogan: Index the diagram by the category of elements of $P$.
steps.detail: Its objects are pairs $(c, x)$ with $x \in P(c)$, and a morphism $(d, x') \to (c, x)$ is a map $g\colon d \to c$ with $P(g)(x) = x'$. The diagram sends $(c, x)$ to the [representable functor](c:representable-functor) $y(c)$ and $g$ to $y(g)$.

steps.slogan: Turn each element $x$ into a map $\hat{x}\colon y(c) \to P$ and check the cocone condition.
steps.detail: The Yoneda lemma gives the natural map $\hat{x}(f) = P(f)(x)$ for $f\colon e \to c$. For $g\colon (d, x') \to (c, x)$, $\hat{x}(g \circ f) = P(f)(P(g)(x)) = \hat{x'}(f)$, so $\hat{x} \circ y(g) = \hat{x'}$.

steps.slogan: Factor any cocone $\lambda$ with vertex $Q$ through $P$ by $\theta_c(x) = \lambda_{(c, x)}(\mathrm{id}_c)$.
steps.detail: For $g\colon d \to c$, the cocone condition and the naturality of $\lambda_{(c, x)}$ give $\theta_d(P(g)(x)) = \lambda_{(c, x)}(g) = Q(g)(\theta_c(x))$, so $\theta\colon P \to Q$ is natural. By the Yoneda lemma $\theta \circ \hat{x} = \lambda_{(c, x)}$, since both send $\mathrm{id}_c$ to the same element.

steps.slogan: Show that the factorization $\theta$ is unique, so the cocone is a colimit.
steps.detail: If $\theta' \circ \hat{x} = \lambda_{(c, x)}$ for all $(c, x)$, then $\theta'_c(x) = \theta'_c(\hat{x}(\mathrm{id}_c)) = \lambda_{(c, x)}(\mathrm{id}_c) = \theta_c(x)$. So the cocone $(\hat{x})$ is a [colimit](c:colimit) cocone and $P \cong \operatorname{colim} y(c)$.

concepts.c:presheaf: The lemma writes an arbitrary presheaf as a colimit.
concepts.c:colimit: The universal property of the colimit is what the proof checks.
concepts.c:representable-functor: The building blocks of the colimit are the representable presheaves.
concepts.c:grothendieck-construction: The category of elements indexes the diagram of representables.

source.note: The standard proof, as in S. Mac Lane, Categories for the Working Mathematician, section III.7 (colimits of representable functors).

statement: For every sentence $\varphi$ of [monadic second-order logic](c:monadic-second-order-logic) on graphs (with quantifiers over vertex sets and edge sets) and every $k$, an [algorithm](c:algorithm) decides whether a [graph](c:graph) $G$ of [treewidth](c:treewidth) at most $k$ satisfies $\varphi$ in time $f(\varphi, k) \cdot n$, where $n$ is the number of vertices of $G$.

hypotheses.text: The property is defined by a fixed sentence $\varphi$ of [monadic second-order logic](c:monadic-second-order-logic) on graphs.
The input graph has [treewidth](c:treewidth) at most a fixed $k$.

conclusion: Whether $G$ satisfies $\varphi$ is decidable in time $f(\varphi, k) \cdot n$.

proofs.name: Tree decomposition and tree automata
proofs.slogan: Compute a tree decomposition, encode the graph as a labeled tree, translate the sentence to trees, and run the tree automaton that the Thatcher–Wright theorem gives.
proofs.scope: An outline of the automata proof in Flum and Grohe; steps 1 and 4 rest on Bodlaender's algorithm and on the Thatcher–Wright theorem, as the cited book shows. A graph of treewidth at most $k$ has at most $kn$ edges, so time linear in $n$ is linear in the input size.

roles.why: Bounded treewidth gives a tree decomposition with bags of at most $k + 1$ vertices, so a finite alphabet encodes the graph.
A monadic second-order sentence on graphs translates into one on labeled trees, which tree automata recognize.

steps.slogan: Compute a tree decomposition of width at most $k$ in linear time.
steps.detail: Bodlaender's [algorithm](c:algorithm) finds, for fixed $k$, a tree decomposition of width at most $k$ of a graph of [treewidth](c:treewidth) at most $k$ in time $f(k) \cdot n$. It can be made binary with $O(n)$ nodes.

steps.slogan: Encode the graph as a tree labeled from a finite alphabet that depends only on $k$.
steps.detail: Name the vertices of each bag by the colors $0, \dots, k$. Label each tree node by the edges inside its bag and by how the colors of its bag match those of its parent; the labeled tree $T_G$ determines $G$.

steps.slogan: Translate $\varphi$ into a monadic second-order sentence $\varphi^*$ about labeled trees.
steps.detail: A vertex set becomes $k + 1$ sets of tree nodes, one per color, that mark where its vertices enter the decomposition; edge sets are handled in the same way. Membership and adjacency are definable from the labels, so $T_G$ satisfies $\varphi^*$ exactly when $G$ satisfies $\varphi$.

steps.slogan: Build a finite bottom-up [tree automaton](c:tree-automaton) that accepts the trees satisfying $\varphi^*$.
steps.detail: By the Thatcher–Wright theorem, the labeled trees that satisfy a monadic second-order sentence form a regular tree language. Its automaton $\mathcal{A}$ depends only on $\varphi$ and $k$, although its size can be non-elementary.

steps.slogan: Run the automaton bottom-up on the encoding tree and accept when the root state is accepting.
steps.detail: Each node gets its state from its label and the states of its children in constant time, so the run takes $O(n)$ steps. With steps 1 to 4 the total time is $f(\varphi, k) \cdot n$.

concepts.c:monadic-second-order-logic: The graph property is a monadic second-order sentence, translated to trees.
concepts.c:algorithm: The theorem gives a linear-time algorithm for each fixed sentence and width.
concepts.c:graph: The input objects are finite graphs.
concepts.c:treewidth: Bounded treewidth lets a finite alphabet encode the graph as a tree.
concepts.c:tree-automaton: A finite tree automaton checks the translated sentence in one pass.

source.ref: J. Flum and M. Grohe, Parameterized Complexity Theory, Texts in Theoretical Computer Science, Springer, Berlin, 2006
source.note: The book proves Courcelle's theorem in its chapter on tree width with the tree automata of its automata-theoretic chapter. Courcelle's original proof (Information and Computation 85, 1990) uses recognizable sets of graphs.

statement: Let $k$ be an [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field) of characteristic $0$. Every pre-Tannakian category $\mathcal{A}$ over $k$ of moderate growth is equivalent to $\operatorname{Rep}(G, \varepsilon)$: the representations on [super vector spaces](c:super-vector-space) of an affine [supergroup](c:supergroup) scheme $G$ on which a fixed $\varepsilon \in G(k)$ with $\varepsilon^2 = 1$ acts as the parity.

hypotheses.text: The field $k$ is [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field) of characteristic $0$.

The category $\mathcal{A}$ is pre-Tannakian: a $k$-linear [abelian category](c:abelian-category) with a rigid [symmetric monoidal](c:symmetric-monoidal-category) structure, $\operatorname{End}(\mathbb{1}) = k$ and objects of finite length.
Each object $X$ has moderate growth: the length of $X^{\otimes n}$ is at most $N_X^n$ for some $N_X$ and all $n$.

conclusion: $\mathcal{A}$ is equivalent to $\operatorname{Rep}(G, \varepsilon)$ as a symmetric tensor category.

proofs.name: Super fiber functor and reconstruction
proofs.slogan: Use moderate growth to kill a Schur functor on each object, split the objects over a commutative ind-algebra to get a super fiber functor, and reconstruct the supergroup.
proofs.scope: An outline of Deligne's 2002 proof (Théorème 0.6); steps 3 to 5 rest on the cited paper and on the Tannakian formalism of Deligne's 1990 Catégories tannakiennes. The nLab page also lists other theorems of Deligne, such as his proof of the Weil conjectures, which are separate records.

roles.why: Characteristic $0$ makes Schur–Weyl decomposition work, and algebraic closure gives a fiber functor over $k$ itself.
The abelian rigid symmetric structure gives Schur functors, commutative ind-algebras and the Tannakian formalism.
Moderate growth bounds the lengths of tensor powers, which forces a Schur functor to vanish on each object.

steps.slogan: Decompose each tensor power $X^{\otimes n}$ into Schur functors of $X$.
steps.detail: The symmetry of $\mathcal{A}$ makes the [symmetric group](c:symmetric-group) $S_n$ act on $X^{\otimes n}$, and in characteristic $0$ this gives $X^{\otimes n} = \bigoplus_{|\lambda| = n} V_\lambda \otimes S_\lambda(X)$. Here $V_\lambda$ is the irreducible representation of $S_n$ and $S_\lambda$ is the [Schur functor](c:schur-functor) of the partition $\lambda$.

steps.slogan: Show that moderate growth makes a Schur functor of rectangular shape kill each object.
steps.detail: If $S_\lambda(X) \ne 0$ for every $\lambda$, the length of $X^{\otimes n}$ is at least $\sum_{|\lambda| = n} \dim V_\lambda$, the number of involutions in $S_n$, which grows faster than every $N^n$. So some $S_\lambda(X) = 0$, and then $S_\mu(X) = 0$ for every $\mu \supseteq \lambda$, in particular for a rectangle with $m + 1$ rows and $n + 1$ columns.

steps.slogan: Build a nonzero commutative ind-algebra over which the object becomes free of rank $(m|n)$.
steps.detail: In $\mathcal{A} \boxtimes \mathrm{sVec}$, which adds an odd unit $\bar{\mathbb{1}}$, Deligne constructs for such an $X$ a faithfully flat commutative algebra $R_X$ in the ind-completion with $R_X \otimes X \cong R_X \otimes (\mathbb{1}^m \oplus \bar{\mathbb{1}}^n)$. The vanishing Schur functor is what makes $R_X$ nonzero.

steps.slogan: Tensor the algebras together and divide by a maximal ideal to get a super fiber functor.
steps.detail: The tensor product $R$ of all $R_X$ is a nonzero commutative ind-algebra, and $X \mapsto R/\mathfrak{m} \otimes X$ for a maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ is a [fiber functor](c:fiber-functor) to super vector spaces over the field $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{1}, R/\mathfrak{m})$. Since $k$ is algebraically closed, the cited paper then gives a super fiber functor $\omega$ with values over $k$.

steps.slogan: Reconstruct the supergroup $G$ of tensor automorphisms of $\omega$ and identify $\mathcal{A}$ with $\operatorname{Rep}(G, \varepsilon)$.
steps.detail: The Tannakian formalism of Catégories tannakiennes, in its super form, makes $G = \underline{\operatorname{Aut}}^{\otimes}(\omega)$ an affine [supergroup](c:supergroup) scheme and $\omega$ an equivalence of $\mathcal{A}$ with representations of $G$. The parity automorphism of $\omega$ is an element $\varepsilon \in G(k)$ with $\varepsilon^2 = 1$, and the symmetry of $\mathcal{A}$ is the super symmetry exactly on $\operatorname{Rep}(G, \varepsilon)$.

concepts.c:algebraically-closed-field: Algebraic closure lets the fiber functor take values over $k$ itself.
concepts.c:super-vector-space: The fiber functor lands in super vector spaces, not ordinary ones.
concepts.c:supergroup: The reconstructed symmetry object is an affine supergroup scheme.
concepts.c:abelian-category: Abelian structure gives lengths, images and the quotients the proof uses.
concepts.c:symmetric-monoidal-category: The symmetry defines the symmetric group action and the Schur functors.
concepts.c:symmetric-group: Its representations count the Schur summands of a tensor power.
concepts.c:schur-functor: A vanishing Schur functor fixes the super dimension of each object.
concepts.c:fiber-functor: The super fiber functor is the input of Tannakian reconstruction.

source.ref: P. Deligne, Catégories tensorielles, Moscow Mathematical Journal 2 (2002), no. 2, 227-248
source.note: Théorème 0.6 of the paper. The reconstruction step uses the Tannakian formalism of P. Deligne, Catégories tannakiennes, in The Grothendieck Festschrift II, Progress in Mathematics 87, Birkhäuser, 1990, 111-195.
